questions.question: In a normal-form game with profile set $S$, when is a profile $s^*\in S$ called Pareto efficient?
options: When $s^*$ Pareto dominates every other profile in $S$
When $s^*$ gives each player the same payoff as the others
When $s^*$ maximises the sum of all players' payoffs on $S$
When no profile in $S$ Pareto dominates $s^*$

questions.question: Two firms are the players of a pricing game. Changing from profile $s'$ to profile $s$ raises both firms' profits but lowers the consumers' surplus. Judged within the game, which statement is correct?
options: $s$ Pareto dominates $s'$: only the players' payoffs count.
It is no Pareto improvement, because the consumers lose out.
$s$ dominates $s'$ only if the firms' gain exceeds the consumers' loss.
The profiles are incomparable, since the change affects outsiders.

questions.question: In a two-player game, play moves from a profile with payoffs $(3,2)$ to another profile with payoffs $(3,4)$. Which statement is correct?
options: This is not a Pareto improvement, since player 1's payoff does not rise.
This is a Pareto improvement: player 2 gains and player 1 loses nothing.
The two profiles are incomparable, as only one of the players gains.
Whether it is one depends on the strategies used, not only on payoffs.

questions.question: View Pareto dominance as a relation on the profile set $S$ of a normal-form game. Which property does this relation fail to have in general?
options: Transitivity: if $s$ dominates $s'$ and $s'$ dominates $s''$, then $s$ may fail to dominate $s''$.
Irreflexivity: a profile can Pareto dominate itself whenever payoffs tie.
Completeness: some pairs of profiles are incomparable.
Asymmetry: two distinct profiles may each Pareto dominate the other one.

questions.question: At profile $s$ of a normal-form game, no single player can raise his own payoff by changing only his own strategy. What follows about the Pareto efficiency of $s$?
options: $s$ is Pareto efficient, because no player is able to do better.
Nothing: some other profile may still be better for every player.
$s$ is Pareto efficient, provided the game has finitely many profiles.
$s$ is never Pareto efficient, as stable profiles are always dominated.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses a row, player 2 a column, and cells list $(v_1,v_2)$: row $T$: $L$: $(3,3)$, $C$: $(0,4)$, $R$: $(2,2)$; row $M$: $L$: $(4,0)$, $C$: $(1,1)$, $R$: $(2,3)$; row $B$: $L$: $(1,2)$, $C$: $(3,1)$, $R$: $(0,5)$. How many of the nine profiles are Pareto efficient?

Player 1 chooses a row, player 2 a column: row $T$: $L$: $(5,0)$, $R$: $(1,1)$; row $B$: $L$: $(2,2)$, $R$: $(0,4)$. The total at $(B,L)$ is $4$, below the total $5$ at $(T,L)$. Is $(B,L)$ Pareto efficient?
options: Yes: no profile gives both players at least $2$ and someone more.
No: $(T,L)$ has the larger total, so it Pareto dominates $(B,L)$.
No: only a profile with the largest total can be Pareto efficient.
Yes, and the reason is that $(B,L)$ gives both players equal payoffs.

questions.question: A game has three players. Four of its profiles give the payoff vectors $a=(2,2,2)$, $b=(3,2,2)$, $c=(4,1,5)$ and $d=(2,3,1)$. Which of $b$, $c$, $d$ Pareto dominate $a$?
options: $b$ and $c$
$c$ only
$b$, $c$ and $d$
$b$ only

questions.question: A profile $s$ of a normal-form game is known to be Pareto efficient. Which conclusion about $s$ is justified?
options: None about single deviations: a player may gain by switching alone.
No player can raise his own payoff by changing only his own strategy.
Each player is at least as well off in $s$ as in any other profile.
$s$ gives the largest possible total payoff among all profiles in $S$.

questions.question: In a finite two-player game, profile $s$ gives player 1 the highest payoff he gets in any profile. Which statement is correct?
options: $s$ is always Pareto efficient, as no profile improves on it for player 1.
$s$ is Pareto efficient only when it also maximises player 2's payoff.
$s$ Pareto dominates every profile giving player 1 a lower payoff.
$s$ can be dominated if another profile ties for player 1 and helps player 2.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses a row, player 2 a column: row $T$: $L$: $(3,2)$, $C$: $(3,4)$, $R$: $(1,5)$; row $B$: $L$: $(4,1)$, $C$: $(2,2)$, $R$: $(4,1)$. How many of the six profiles are Pareto efficient?

Player 1 chooses a row, player 2 a column: row $T$: $L$: $(4,1)$, $R$: $(1,1)$; row $B$: $L$: $(2,4)$, $R$: $(0,0)$. Now every payoff of player 1 is multiplied by $3$, player 2's payoffs unchanged. What happens?
options: Both the efficient set and the total-maximising profile stay exactly the same.
The efficient set stays $\{(T,L),(B,L)\}$, but the total-maximising profile changes.
The efficient set shrinks to $\{(T,L)\}$, the profile with the new largest total.
The efficient set changes, because the payoff totals of the profiles change.
